subtype: Approach: consult a trusted family member or a registered adviser [Action]
passage: At the bus stop in a small town in Bihar, Tushar showed a printed pamphlet to an uncle who worked in a bank. It promised a doubled sum in a year and had no company address. The uncle read it slowly and shook his head. "Where is the paperwork? Who is the seller? Who checks them?" On Saturday Tushar took the same pamphlet to Rukmini, a registered adviser with a small office near the market. Rukmini looked at it for a minute and said no genuine product doubles money that fast, and that a real firm would give papers and a registration number. Tushar walked out lighter. When the pamphlet-seller called that evening, Tushar said politely, "No, thank you. I have checked, and the answer is no."

qa.q: Who did Tushar show the pamphlet to first?
qa.a: Tushar showed the pamphlet first to an uncle who worked in a bank.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel when saying no to the seller?
qa.a: Tushar felt lighter and confident, since two people had pointed to the same problems.

qa.q: What could Tushar do if the seller keeps calling, and why?
qa.a: Tushar could stop answering and tell the uncle, because repeated pressure is a warning sign.

qa.q: How might the uncle see a young relative bringing the pamphlet?
qa.a: The uncle probably feels glad to be asked and worried about the pamphlet, and points out missing paperwork.

grounding: A student shows the offer to an uncle who works in a bank and to a registered adviser, and both point out unrealistic returns and no paperwork.

subtype: Approach: consult a trusted family member or a registered adviser [Action]
passage:
The flyer had been slipped under every door in Jin's student residence in Manchester: 'Property fund, 3% a month, minimum £500, spaces filling fast.' A smiling man at the campus café had already given her a card.
Jin didn't sign. She did two things first. On Saturday she video-called her uncle Jamal, who has worked at a bank in Leeds for twenty years, and held the flyer up to the camera. He read it twice. 'Three percent a month is over forty a year,' he said. 'And where's the fund's registration? Where's any document at all?'
On Monday she booked a free session at the university's money advice centre, with a registered adviser. The adviser asked the same thing: 'Can they show you any paperwork?' They couldn't; she'd already emailed and got only a voice note back.
On Tuesday, when the man at the café asked, Jin said, 'No, thank you,' and didn't need to explain.

qa.q: What return did the flyer promise?
How did Jin feel saying no on Tuesday?
qa.a: Jin felt confident and calm, sure enough after both checks that no explanation was needed.
Asking two people she could trust, her uncle and a registered adviser, before paying anything; both spotted the same missing paperwork.

qa.q: How does the flyer look to Jamal?
qa.a: Jamal sees an unrealistic return and no registration, two warning signs a banker would spot at once.

grounding: Shows a student showing an offer to an uncle who works in a bank and to a registered adviser, and declining with confidence.

subtype: Approach: consult a trusted family member or a registered adviser [Action]
passage:
The college's financial-literacy cell held drop-in hours on Thursdays, in a small room behind the library. Rehana came in with a printout of a chat: a classmate's 'wealth mentor' offering 'assured 8% monthly' on a crypto plan, joining fee ₹15,000.
She had already sent it the night before to her Mamu, who works at a bank branch in Lucknow. His reply was short: 'No company can promise this. Ask them for their registration and a signed agreement. They won't have it.'
Now she wanted a second view. Rekha, the registered adviser who volunteers at the cell, read the printout slowly. 'Assured, and monthly. So ask: where's the paperwork?' Rehana showed the chat where she had asked. The mentor had replied, 'Trust the process.'
'That's your answer,' Rekha said.
Rehana typed her reply to the classmate right there: 'Not joining. Thanks.' Her hands were steady.

qa.q: What do Rehana's steady hands suggest?
qa.a: She feels confident and settled, because two people she trusted saw the same warning signs.

qa.q: Why was it helpful to ask both Mamu and Rekha?
qa.a: Mamu knows banking and Rekha is a registered adviser; hearing the same warning from both let Rehana decline with confidence.

qa.q: How might the classmate see Rehana's short reply?
qa.a: The classmate may be disappointed or push again, but the plain reply leaves little room to argue.

grounding: Shows a student checking an offer with a family member at a bank and a registered adviser, who both point to unrealistic returns and no paperwork.
